Final deliverable — only the two flagged sentences corrected; all other content unchanged.

**Section 4.1 (size ladder) — corrected sentence:**
"Proposed ladder: N_train ∈ {64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048} (log₂-spaced, doubling).

**Why 64 is a defensible lower bound (corrected):** with d = 28 model inputs, 2d = 56, so 64 lies **just above 2d** (N/d ≈ 2.3), and is still far below the common heuristic of roughly ten samples per parameter (10d ≈ 280). This is **intentional**: the lowest levels are chosen to sit in the **data-poor regime** — only a few samples per feature — where architectures are expected to diverge most (underfitting vs. overfitting behaviour). Starting here makes the early, steep part of the learning curve visible."

**Section 8, L2 (column count / body-style placement) — corrected sentence:**
"L2 / A2 (column count / body-style placement). Conclusions about '26 parameters' and the data-poor lower bound depend on d. The lower bound 64 corresponds to N/d ≈ 2.3 for d = 28 (just above 2d = 56). *If body-style is counted among the 26 (d = 26 incl. categorical) or the continuous count differs, the feature dimension, the N/d ≈ 2.3 lower-bound justification, and the GP high-dimension expectation all shift.* Design re-anchors to the real schema before execution."

All other sections (1 Research question and hypothesis; 2 Data description and assumptions; 3 Surrogate architectures and rationale; 4.2–4.4 sampling, controls (S = 20 seeds, test set = max(0.20·N_total, 512)), execution structure; 5 Evaluation protocol and metrics; 6 Statistical analysis plan (LMM primary + paired Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-corrected); 7 Feasibility and compute estimate (GP Cholesky ≈ 2.9×10⁹ flops at N=2048, ~100 parallel jobs on 224 cores, fallback cap at 1024 / sparse GP); 8 remaining limitations L1, L3–L7) are unchanged and acceptable as previously written.

context.question: Does the predictive performance of surrogate models based on parametric data improve with increased training set size and differ across model architectures in aerodynamic drag prediction? This experiment uses aerodynamic car designs characterized by 26 parameters—as provided in the DrivAerNet++ dataset, which includes diverse configurations such as fastback, notchback, and estateback—for assessing performance scalability and model-specific behavior.
